(B) The Mongols were ideological feminists committed to complete gender equality in every sphere
(C) Women served only as warriors
(D) Islamic law required female equality
explanation: Pastoral nomadism made women's work indispensable: with men away herding or at war, women ran the mobile household, managed herds, and controlled property. Economic necessity gave Mongol women a public authority that sedentary patriarchies denied.

stem: Boorstin says the 'dominant Island of the Earth' was displaced by a 'dominant Ocean.' What shift is he describing?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Daniel Boorstin, The Discoverers (1983): Within decades of Columbus's voyages, the European world was transformed. The dominant Island of the Earth, the connected landmass of Afro-Eurasia, was displaced by a dominant Ocean of the Earth, the connected body of water covering most of the surface. Never had the arena of human experience been so suddenly revised.
options: (A) The oceans dried up
(B) Oceanic networks displaced overland Afro-Eurasian routes as dominant
(C) All land trade ended permanently
(D) Europe sank beneath the sea, permanently ending its role in global trade networks
explanation: For millennia the great trade networks ran overland across Afro-Eurasia, the 'Island of the Earth.' After 1492 the oceans became the highways: silver, sugar, slaves, and ideas moved by sea, and maritime powers displaced the old land empires as the centers of world trade.

stem: The caravel combined square sails with lateen sails. Why did this matter for exploration?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Daniel Boorstin, The Discoverers (1983): Within decades of Columbus's voyages, the European world was transformed. The dominant Island of the Earth, the connected landmass of Afro-Eurasia, was displaced by a dominant Ocean of the Earth, the connected body of water covering most of the surface. Never had the arena of human experience been so suddenly revised.
options: (A) It was the largest ship ever built
(B) Its hybrid sails let it sail both with and against prevailing winds
(C) It carried only cannons, no sails
(D) Sail design was irrelevant to exploration; only cannons and hull size mattered
explanation: Square sails drove ships before the wind; lateen sails let them tack against it. The caravel's hybrid rig could do both, freeing Portuguese sailors from the wind patterns that had trapped earlier vessels and opening the Atlantic to systematic exploration.

stem: Mercantilists believed a nation must export more than it imports. Why?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Daniel Boorstin, The Discoverers (1983): Within decades of Columbus's voyages, the European world was transformed. The dominant Island of the Earth, the connected landmass of Afro-Eurasia, was displaced by a dominant Ocean of the Earth, the connected body of water covering most of the surface. Never had the arena of human experience been so suddenly revised.
options: (A) Imports are more valuable than exports because they bring desirable foreign goods home
(B) Gold and silver are worthless
(C) Trade policy does not matter
(D) Trade surpluses would be paid in gold and silver, the measure of power
explanation: Mercantilists equated national power with hoards of gold and silver. A favorable balance of trade, selling more than buying, would be settled in bullion flowing into the treasury, so governments promoted exports, restricted imports, and seized colonies as sources of precious metal.

stem: The Manila galleons carried Chinese porcelain to Mexico and Mexican silver to Asia for 250 years. What does this show?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Daniel Boorstin, The Discoverers (1983): Within decades of Columbus's voyages, the European world was transformed. The dominant Island of the Earth, the connected landmass of Afro-Eurasia, was displaced by a dominant Ocean of the Earth, the connected body of water covering most of the surface. Never had the arena of human experience been so suddenly revised.
options: (A) Asia was isolated from world trade
(B) Mexican silver never left the Americas, piling up uselessly in colonial vaults
(C) A single commercial circuit linked Asia, the Americas, and Europe
(D) The galleons sailed only once
explanation: For two and a half centuries the galleons linked three continents: American silver bought Asian silks, spices, and porcelain, which sailed to Acapulco and on to Europe. A single commercial circuit bound Manila, Mexico City, and Seville together, the first truly global trade network.

stem: Japan's victory over China in 1894-95 demonstrated which result of the Meiji reforms?
stimulus: A modern historian summarizes Japan's transformation: after decades of weakness, it was good to be Japanese at last, and to humble the mighty neighbor that had dominated the horizon for so long. In under forty years, Japan had gone from a feudal society to a modern state — with advanced weaponry, a professional military bureaucracy, reformed governing structures, and a new educational system reaching the whole population.
options: (A) China possessed no modern weapons at all
(B) Meiji reforms made Japan modern
(C) European troops fought on Japan's behalf
(D) The war was fought over control of Taiwan
explanation: In 1894-95 Japan's modern conscript army and navy defeated Qing China, the 'mighty neighbor' that had dominated East Asia for centuries. The victory proved that four decades of Meiji reform — modern weaponry, a military bureaucracy, new governing structures, and mass schooling — had transformed a feudal society into a modern power. (A) is wrong because China did possess some modern arms; Japan's edge was institutional, not a Chinese vacuum. (C) is wrong because no European troops fought for Japan in this war. (D) is wrong because the war was fought over Korea; Taiwan was seized as a prize afterward, not the original cause.

stem: The Meiji slogan 'rich country, strong army' (fukoku kyohei) best reflects which priority of the new government?
stimulus: A modern historian summarizes Japan's transformation: after decades of weakness, it was good to be Japanese at last, and to humble the mighty neighbor that had dominated the horizon for so long. In under forty years, Japan had gone from a feudal society to a modern state — with advanced weaponry, a professional military bureaucracy, reformed governing structures, and a new educational system reaching the whole population.
options: (A) Industrial and military strength to resist the West
(B) Restoring the shogun's traditional authority
(C) Making Japan fully self-sufficient in raw materials
(D) Spreading democratic government throughout Japan
explanation: Fukoku kyohei meant building the economic and military muscle to stand up to the Western powers, end the humiliation of the unequal treaties, and keep Japan from suffering China's fate. Every Meiji reform — industry, conscription, education — served that defensive modernization. (B) is wrong because the Meiji reforms destroyed the shogunate rather than restoring it. (C) is wrong because Japan knew it could never supply all raw materials domestically; the goal was strength, not autarky. (D) is wrong because the Meiji state was oligarchic, not democratic.

stem: Why did governments across the industrializing world subsidize railroad construction even when private investors hesitated?
options: (A) Railroads could never turn a profit without permanent charity
(B) Railroads linked resources, factories, and markets into integrated national economies
(C) Railroads were built mainly to serve passenger tourism
(D) Governments built railroads mainly to provide salaried jobs for aristocrats and officials
explanation: Factories were useless without coal and iron reaching them and finished goods reaching buyers. Railroads stitched mines, mills, farms, and ports into single national markets, and because the upfront costs were enormous and returns slow, governments from Russia to Japan to the United States subsidized them. (A) is wrong because railroads were ultimately profitable; the issue was the scale of initial investment. (C) is wrong because freight, not tourism, was the economic engine of early railroads. (D) is wrong because governments subsidized railroads for economic and strategic reasons, not to employ aristocrats.

stem: Smith argued that individuals pursuing their own profit are 'led by an invisible hand' to benefit society. What did he mean?
stimulus: An economist of the Scottish Enlightenment argued that when any trade is left open to free competition, the public gains the most. Each person chasing their own advantage is led, as if by an invisible hand, to serve ends they never intended — cheaper and better goods for everyone.
options: (A) A secret government committee guides market outcomes
(B) Businessmen are morally superior to other citizens
(C) All business profits should be donated to the state
(D) Competition lowers prices and improves goods
explanation: Smith's invisible hand is the claim that competition disciplines self-interest: each producer chasing profit must cut prices and improve quality to win customers, so the public gains better, cheaper goods without any official directing the process. (A) is wrong because the invisible hand is precisely the absence of any directing committee. (B) is wrong because Smith made no claim about businessmen's moral superiority; the mechanism works regardless of character. (C) is wrong because Smith opposed state confiscation of profits; the hand works through private gain, not charity.

stem: Industrialization popularized the ideal of 'separate spheres' for men and women. What did this ideal claim?
options: (A) Women should work in factories while men manage the household
(B) Men belonged to public work and politics; women belonged to domestic life
(C) Industrial society abolished distinct gender roles
(D) Children should leave school and become the family's primary earners in factories
explanation: As work moved from homes to factories and mines, middle-class ideology split life into two spheres: the competitive public world of men and the sheltered domestic world of women, whose proper role became wife and mother rather than wage earner. (A) is wrong because the ideal assigned factory and political life to men, not women. (C) is wrong because separate spheres reinforced gender distinctions rather than abolishing them. (D) is wrong because child labor was a separate industrial phenomenon, not the content of the separate-spheres ideal.

stem: Criollos were wealthy, American-born Spaniards. Why did many of them support independence from Spain?
stimulus: In colonial Latin America, 'caste' came to mean racial lineage. Spanish elites constructed a hierarchy of peninsulares (Spaniards born in Spain), criollos (Spaniards born in the Americas), mestizos, and mulatos. Both the colonial state and the Church demanded heavier taxes and tribute from the lower categories. The obsession with purity of blood reached back to Spain's centuries of reconquest from Muslim rule, when Christian ancestry became a badge of status — an idea transplanted to the Americas and fastened onto skin color and birthplace.
options: (A) They were enslaved and sought personal freedom
(B) Peninsulares blocked criollos from high office
(C) They wanted to restore the Aztec empire
(D) Spain taxed criollos heavily while exempting peninsulares
explanation: Criollos were American-born Spaniards of pure Spanish ancestry — wealthy and educated, yet barred from the viceroyalties, audiencias, and bishoprics reserved for peninsulares born in Spain. That glass ceiling turned an otherwise privileged group into revolutionaries. (A) is wrong because criollos were among the wealthiest people in the colonies, not an enslaved class. (C) is wrong because the movement sought independence from Spain, not a restoration of the Aztec empire. (D) is wrong because the grievance was exclusion from high office, not a tax distinction between the two Spanish groups.

stem: Spanish America's obsession with 'purity of blood' originated in which earlier Spanish experience?
stimulus: In colonial Latin America, 'caste' came to mean racial lineage. Spanish elites constructed a hierarchy of peninsulares (Spaniards born in Spain), criollos (Spaniards born in the Americas), mestizos, and mulatos. Both the colonial state and the Church demanded heavier taxes and tribute from the lower categories. The obsession with purity of blood reached back to Spain's centuries of reconquest from Muslim rule, when Christian ancestry became a badge of status — an idea transplanted to the Americas and fastened onto skin color and birthplace.
options: (A) The Inquisition's trials and persecution of Protestants across Europe
(B) The centuries-long Reconquista against Muslim rule in Iberia
(C) Aztec tribute lists
(D) The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767
explanation: Limpieza de sangre — 'purity of blood' — was forged during the Reconquista, when centuries of war against Muslim kingdoms made unmixed Christian ancestry a mark of honor and a qualification for office. Spaniards carried that mental framework to the Americas, where it hardened into the casta system ranking people by birthplace and ancestry. (A) is wrong because the Inquisition's pursuit of Protestants came later and was a different campaign. (C) is wrong because Aztec tribute lists recorded goods owed, not Spanish ideas of blood purity. (D) is wrong because the Jesuit expulsion of 1767 had nothing to do with the origins of the purity obsession.

stem: Wordsworth wrote as a young witness of 1789; Dickens wrote decades later, after the Terror. What does their difference illustrate about historical interpretation?
stimulus: Paraphrase of two literary responses to the French Revolution: Charles Dickens, writing in 1859, opens with famous paired opposites, calling the age of revolution simultaneously the best and worst of times, an age of wisdom and of foolishness, a season of light and of darkness, a spring of hope and a winter of despair. William Wordsworth, remembering his youth during the Revolution's opening, writes simply that it was bliss to be alive in that dawn, and to be young was very heaven.
options: (A) Older writers always judge the past more accurately
(B) Poetry is useless as historical evidence
(C) The Revolution had no genuine supporters
(D) A writer's moment in time and personal experience shape judgment of the same event
explanation: Wordsworth wrote in the dawn of 1789 as a young sympathizer, drunk on hope; Dickens wrote in 1859 with the Terror, the guillotine, and Napoleon's empire in full view. The same Revolution looks different from inside its hopeful opening than from after its violent sequel, showing how a writer's moment and experience color judgment of the past.

stem: Both the American and French Revolutions protested unfair taxation. In which crucial respect did the French Revolution differ from the American?
stimulus: Paraphrase of two literary responses to the French Revolution: Charles Dickens, writing in 1859, opens with famous paired opposites, calling the age of revolution simultaneously the best and worst of times, an age of wisdom and of foolishness, a season of light and of darkness, a spring of hope and a winter of despair. William Wordsworth, remembering his youth during the Revolution's opening, writes simply that it was bliss to be alive in that dawn, and to be young was very heaven.
options: (A) Only the American Revolution involved taxation
(B) France had no tax grievances
(C) Both revolutions immediately restored their monarchies within a few years of republican rule
(D) The French Revolution overturned the entire social order; the American kept its elites
explanation: American colonists kept their property structure and much of their elite; the French revolutionaries abolished feudal dues, seized Church lands, and executed the king, attempting to remake the social order from the ground up. One was a war of independence, the other a social revolution.

stem: Robespierre justified the Terror as the necessary companion of virtue. What logic did this express?
stimulus: Paraphrase of two literary responses to the French Revolution: Charles Dickens, writing in 1859, opens with famous paired opposites, calling the age of revolution simultaneously the best and worst of times, an age of wisdom and of foolishness, a season of light and of darkness, a spring of hope and a winter of despair. William Wordsworth, remembering his youth during the Revolution's opening, writes simply that it was bliss to be alive in that dawn, and to be young was very heaven.
options: (A) He opposed all political violence
(B) Revolutionary virtue required terror against the republic's enemies
(C) He sought to restore the monarchy
(D) The Terror was an unintended accident
explanation: Robespierre argued that the Revolution's virtue, its devotion to the public good, could not survive against its enemies, royalists, hoarders, traitors, without terror to crush them: virtue wedded to terror would save the republic. It was the classic logic of ends justifying extreme means.

stem: How did Enlightenment social-contract ideas undermine absolute monarchy?
stimulus: Paraphrase of two literary responses to the French Revolution: Charles Dickens, writing in 1859, opens with famous paired opposites, calling the age of revolution simultaneously the best and worst of times, an age of wisdom and of foolishness, a season of light and of darkness, a spring of hope and a winter of despair. William Wordsworth, remembering his youth during the Revolution's opening, writes simply that it was bliss to be alive in that dawn, and to be young was very heaven.
options: (A) By claiming legitimacy comes from the people's consent, not divine right
(B) By proving that kings were immortal
(C) By supporting the divine right of kings as the only God-given form of authority
(D) By opposing all forms of government
explanation: Enlightenment thinkers argued that governments rest on a contract with the governed, who retain natural rights. That claim pulled the rug from under divine-right monarchy: if legitimacy comes from consent, an absolute king ruling without it is a usurper by definition.

stem: Toussaint reports Sonthonax's murder plot to the Directory while refusing to join it. What does this show about Toussaint's strategy?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Toussaint L'Ouverture's 1797 report to the French Directory, recounting his conversation with Commissioner Sonthonax: Sonthonax tells Toussaint, the colony's black inhabitants fear for their freedom, and the suspicious white colonists must all be slaughtered; everything is ready, needing only Toussaint's agreement. Toussaint reacts with disbelief. The next morning Sonthonax returns to the scheme, saying they are perfectly placed to act and that Toussaint's influence over the people makes him the ideal partner. Toussaint accuses him of trying to ruin him: killing the whites, seizing independence, after promising never to raise such projects again. Sonthonax backtracks, claiming he only means expulsion, not murder, but Toussaint notes the contradiction and warns that any white death would be blamed on him. Sonthonax swears never to speak of it again and begs Toussaint to keep the secret from his own officers. Toussaint coldly gives his word and takes his leave.
options: (A) He was a naive pawn of the French
(B) He posed as France's loyal defender of order while building his own power
(C) He wanted to restore slavery and return Saint-Domingue to the plantation system
(D) He had no political strategy
explanation: Toussaint sends the Directory a report showing Sonthonax plotting murder while Toussaint refuses, a document that simultaneously proves his loyalty to France, discredits a rival, and demonstrates that he, not the commissioner, holds real power in Saint-Domingue. He serves France while making himself indispensable.

stem: Toussaint wrote this exchange up in dialogue form and sent it to the French Directory. What political work was the report doing for him?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Toussaint L'Ouverture's 1797 report to the French Directory, recounting his conversation with Commissioner Sonthonax: Sonthonax tells Toussaint, the colony's black inhabitants fear for their freedom, and the suspicious white colonists must all be slaughtered; everything is ready, needing only Toussaint's agreement. Toussaint reacts with disbelief. The next morning Sonthonax returns to the scheme, saying they are perfectly placed to act and that Toussaint's influence over the people makes him the ideal partner. Toussaint accuses him of trying to ruin him: killing the whites, seizing independence, after promising never to raise such projects again. Sonthonax backtracks, claiming he only means expulsion, not murder, but Toussaint notes the contradiction and warns that any white death would be blamed on him. Sonthonax swears never to speak of it again and begs Toussaint to keep the secret from his own officers. Toussaint coldly gives his word and takes his leave.
options: (A) It was a private diary, never intended for any reader
(B) It urged the Directory to restore slavery in Saint-Domingue
(C) It discredited a rival commissioner while advertising Toussaint's own loyalty to France
(D) It asked the Directory to execute Sonthonax at once
explanation: The report is a political document dressed as a transcript: Sonthonax appears as a murderous schemer, Toussaint as the loyal officer who refuses him. Sent to the government in Paris, it undercuts a rival who outranked him while proving that the colony's real power — and its reliable servant — was Toussaint himself. (A) is wrong because the report was addressed to the Directory. (B) is wrong because Toussaint built his power on the end of slavery. (D) is wrong because the report asks for no execution; it works by implication, not demand.

stem: Toussaint wrote this report to the French Directory about his own loyalty and Sonthonax's treachery. What should historians consider when using it?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Toussaint L'Ouverture's 1797 report to the French Directory, recounting his conversation with Commissioner Sonthonax: Sonthonax tells Toussaint, the colony's black inhabitants fear for their freedom, and the suspicious white colonists must all be slaughtered; everything is ready, needing only Toussaint's agreement. Toussaint reacts with disbelief. The next morning Sonthonax returns to the scheme, saying they are perfectly placed to act and that Toussaint's influence over the people makes him the ideal partner. Toussaint accuses him of trying to ruin him: killing the whites, seizing independence, after promising never to raise such projects again. Sonthonax backtracks, claiming he only means expulsion, not murder, but Toussaint notes the contradiction and warns that any white death would be blamed on him. Sonthonax swears never to speak of it again and begs Toussaint to keep the secret from his own officers. Toussaint coldly gives his word and takes his leave.
options: (A) The report is self-serving: Toussaint had reason to paint himself as loyal
(B) The report is perfectly objective
(C) Toussaint was illiterate
(D) The Directory could not read French and relied entirely on translators for all reports
explanation: The report is Toussaint's own account of his own virtue, sent to the government whose favor he needs. He has every incentive to make Sonthonax look treacherous and himself look loyal, so historians must read it as advocacy, not as a neutral transcript.

stem: The First Fleet (1788) carried marines, officials, and hundreds of male and female convicts. Why did Britain need a penal colony on the other side of the world?
stimulus: The chart of the First Fleet (1788) lists the colony's human cargo: marines and their families, male and female convicts, and officials, with notes on supplies, livestock, and the colony's first difficult years.
options: (A) Britain wanted to free its convicts
(B) Australia invited British convicts to settle and develop its empty coastline freely
(C) With America closed after 1776, Britain needed somewhere to exile convicts
(D) The First Fleet carried tourists
explanation: After American independence closed the old dumping ground, Britain's prisons and prison hulks overflowed with convicts. Australia offered a distant shore where the unwanted could be shipped beyond return, solving a domestic crisis of crime and punishment.

stem: The First Fleet's colony nearly starved in its first years despite bringing farmers and seed. What does this show about settler colonialism?
stimulus: The chart of the First Fleet (1788) lists the colony's human cargo: marines and their families, male and female convicts, and officials, with notes on supplies, livestock, and the colony's first difficult years.
options: (A) European farming methods failed in unfamiliar Australian conditions
(B) Australia was an easy paradise for farmers, with rich soil and gentle rains
(C) The convicts refused to eat
(D) Britain supplied the colony generously
explanation: The settlement nearly starved: unfamiliar soils, erratic rain, and English farming methods that failed in Australian conditions. The colony survived only by learning, slowly and painfully, to farm a continent that obeyed different rules.

stem: The First Fleet chart lists convicts, marines, supplies, and livestock. What kind of historical source is it, and what is it most useful for?
stimulus: The chart of the First Fleet (1788) lists the colony's human cargo: marines and their families, male and female convicts, and officials, with notes on supplies, livestock, and the colony's first difficult years.
options: (A) A novel about colonial life
(B) A scientific study of Australian ecology, wildlife, and native plant species
(C) A religious text
(D) An administrative record useful for studying logistics and hardship
explanation: The chart is a bureaucratic manifest: headcounts of convicts and marines, lists of supplies and livestock. It reveals what administrators counted, logistics, not what colonists felt, making it evidence for material hardship rather than for inner experience.

stem: In 1791 Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, mirroring the Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man. What was her argument?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Olympe de Gouges's Reflections on Slavery (1788): The law of nature was never more visible: people are equal everywhere. But Europeans, thirsting for blood and for the gold that greed worships, have transformed these happy lands. If the enslaved are animals, are we not animals too? How do whites differ from blacks? Only in color. Why do blonds not claim superiority over brunettes? Why is the mulatto not superior to the black? As nature produces varied animals, plants, and minerals, so human color varies. Does the day quarrel with the night, the sun with the moon? All things differ, and therein lies nature's beauty; why destroy its work? When submission flags, the islanders' barbaric despotism breeds revolts, poisonings, and every atrocity of the oppressed. Is it not monstrous that Europeans, enriched by others' exploitation, have blacks flogged morning to night? These souls would work no less with more freedom and kindness.
options: (A) Women should remain in the domestic sphere and avoid all political activity forever
(B) The Revolution should be overthrown
(C) Slavery should be preserved
(D) The Revolution's universal rights must include women or it betrays itself
explanation: The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed liberty and equality while the Assembly denied both to women. De Gouges turned the Revolution's own logic against it: if rights are truly universal and natural, excluding half of humanity is a contradiction that destroys the Revolution's legitimacy.

(B) It restored slavery

explanation: The American, French, and Latin American revolutions were led by elites seeking political independence; only in Saint-Domingue did the enslaved themselves rise, defeat the planters, the French, the British, and the Spanish, and found a Black republic. Haiti stands alone as revolution from below.

stem: Bolivar writes that Americans are 'neither Indian nor European, but a species midway between.' What problem was he describing?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Simon Bolivar's Jamaica Letter (1815): Sixteen million Americans suffer Spanish repression, though Spain is now too weak to rule the hemisphere. We are a young people in the arts and sciences, yet old in civilized society, retaining scarcely a vestige of what once was. We are neither Indian nor European but midway between the legitimate proprietors of the country and the Spanish usurpers; though American by birth, we derive our rights from Europe. Spain's monarchs made a solemn compact with the conquerors and settlers, making them lords of the land with vast privileges, while the king kept only sovereign domain. Today Americans live no better than serfs, forbidden to grow European crops, to trade freely, or to build manufactures, while royal monopolies and barriers between provinces stifle all exchange. The provinces fight for freedom and will succeed; some will form republics, the larger may become monarchies, and some will collapse in revolutions.
options: (A) He praised Spanish colonial society
(B) He wanted to be European
(C) Identity was irrelevant to independence and played no role in his political thought
(D) Colonial society had a fractured identity, belonging fully to neither world
explanation: Criollos were American-born Spaniards: legally Spanish, yet treated as second-class by peninsulares and surrounded by Indigenous and African peoples they neither fully belonged to nor ruled justly. Bolívar names the identity crisis at the heart of Spanish American nation-building: new nations had to be invented from a population that was neither one thing nor the other.

stem: Bolivar calls Indigenous peoples the 'legitimate proprietors' yet led a criollo movement that kept them subordinated. What tension does this reveal?

(B) Indigenous peoples led the independence wars and wrote the new republics' constitutions
(C) He invoked Indigenous legitimacy while keeping Indigenous peoples subordinated
(D) There was no tension in his position
explanation: Bolívar's armies were criollo-led and his republics preserved large estates and forced Indigenous labor. Invoking the 'legitimate proprietors' gave his cause moral grandeur, but independence transferred power from peninsulares to criollos, leaving Indigenous peoples dispossessed under new masters.

stem: Bolivar describes the conquistadors' agreement with the Spanish king as 'our social contract.' What is he doing with this Enlightenment language?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Simon Bolivar's Jamaica Letter (1815): Sixteen million Americans suffer Spanish repression, though Spain is now too weak to rule the hemisphere. We are a young people in the arts and sciences, yet old in civilized society, retaining scarcely a vestige of what once was. We are neither Indian nor European but midway between the legitimate proprietors of the country and the Spanish usurpers; though American by birth, we derive our rights from Europe. Spain's monarchs made a solemn compact with the conquerors and settlers, making them lords of the land with vast privileges, while the king kept only sovereign domain. Today Americans live no better than serfs, forbidden to grow European crops, to trade freely, or to build manufactures, while royal monopolies and barriers between provinces stifle all exchange. The provinces fight for freedom and will succeed; some will form republics, the larger may become monarchies, and some will collapse in revolutions.
options: (A) He framed the colonial compact as a contract Spain broke, justifying rebellion
(B) He defended the Spanish king as America's only legitimate sovereign against all rebels
(C) He rejected all contract theory
(D) He praised feudal privilege
explanation: Locke and Rousseau argued that governments are legitimate only by the consent of the governed, who entrust rulers with power for the common good. Bolívar casts the original compact between the Spanish king and the settlers as exactly such a contract, and Spain's violation of it, monopolies, trade barriers, serf-like subjection, as the breach that dissolves obedience.

stem: The Berlin Act pledged to protect native peoples' welfare, yet the Congo Free State became a byword for atrocity. What does this gap best illustrate about New Imperialism?
stimulus: Article VI of the 1885 Berlin Act bound the signatory powers to watch over the preservation of native tribes in their African territories and to care for the improvement of the tribes' moral and material well-being, including help in suppressing slavery. The powers further pledged to protect, without distinction of creed or nation, all religious, scientific, and charitable institutions organized to instruct the native population and advance these ends.
options: (A) European powers sincerely made native welfare their top priority
(B) Moral cover for economic exploitation
(C) The Berlin Act banned all colonial trade in Africa
(D) Missionaries controlled the conference's decisions
explanation: The Berlin Act wrapped the partition of Africa in humanitarian language — protecting native tribes, improving their moral and material welfare, suppressing slavery — while the powers' real business was dividing markets, mines, and strategic territory. The Congo Free State, personally owned by Leopold II, became the most notorious case of atrocity committed under that cover. (A) is wrong because the record of forced labor and mutilation in the Congo disproves sincere humanitarian priority. (C) is wrong because the Act regulated rather than banned colonial commerce. (D) is wrong because missionaries did not control the conference; diplomats dividing Africa did.

stem: David Livingstone promoted 'Christianity, commerce, and civilization' as the cure for Africa's ills. How did this formula actually serve imperial expansion?
stimulus: Article VI of the 1885 Berlin Act bound the signatory powers to watch over the preservation of native tribes in their African territories and to care for the improvement of the tribes' moral and material well-being, including help in suppressing slavery. The powers further pledged to protect, without distinction of creed or nation, all religious, scientific, and charitable institutions organized to instruct the native population and advance these ends.
options: (A) It single-handedly ended the African slave trade
(B) It established Africans as equal partners in colonial rule
(C) It won domestic support by portraying empire as moral uplift
(D) It opposed any European presence in Africa
explanation: Livingstone's formula framed empire as a moral mission — ending slavery, spreading the gospel, opening 'legitimate' commerce — which made colonial ventures respectable to British voters, churches, and Parliament, securing the political support imperialism needed. (A) is wrong because the slave trade's suppression took decades of naval enforcement, not one man's slogan. (B) is wrong because the formula assumed European superiority and tutelage, not partnership. (D) is wrong because the 3 Cs justified European presence rather than opposing it.

stem: In a 1939 film set in 1885, a character says the hero and heroine are 'saved from the blessings of civilization' as they flee the reach of corrupt lawmen. What irony does this sarcastic usage highlight?
stimulus: In John Ford's 1939 Western Stagecoach, a stagecoach crosses dangerous Apache territory carrying a mixed group of passengers: a drunken doctor, a gambler, a prostitute, a timid whiskey salesman, and a proper banker's wife. The outlaw Ringo Kid joins them, seeking revenge on the men who framed him. The film's last line, spoken as the hero and heroine ride beyond the reach of the town's corrupt sheriff and respectable hypocrites: 'Well -- they're saved from the blessings of civilization.'
options: (A) Civilization always brings genuine freedom
(B) The frontier had no law or institutions at all
(C) The character sincerely praises the blessings of the legal system
(D) So-called civilized institutions can be corrupt
explanation: The line is sarcastic: the hero and heroine are fleeing the corrupt institutions of 'civilization' — its courts and lawmen — so being 'saved' from civilization's blessings means escaping into freedom. The irony is that the very institutions claiming to embody civilization can be corrupt and oppressive. (A) is wrong because the sarcasm undercuts any claim that civilization automatically brings freedom. (B) is wrong because the frontier in the film does have law — corrupt law, which is the point. (C) is wrong because the tone is plainly mocking, not praising.

stem: Why did the Congo Free State produce some of the worst atrocities of the New Imperialism era?
options: (A) Belgian settlers sought farmland and seized Congolese villages
(B) Missionary societies competed violently for converts
(C) Leopold's agents enforced rubber quotas by terror
(D) A prolonged drought destroyed the region's food supply
explanation: Leopold II ran the Congo as his personal property, and his agents — backed by the Force Publique — forced villagers to meet rubber quotas through hostage-taking, whipping, and mutilation. The profit-driven quota system, not settlement or climate, produced the atrocities. (A) is wrong because the Congo was exploited for rubber and ivory, not settled for farmland. (B) is wrong because missionaries did not drive the violence. (D) is wrong because the catastrophe was man-made, not caused by drought.

stem: British investors financed Argentine railroads and Chilean mines in the 1800s. What pattern did this investment create?
options: (A) Latin America industrialized ahead of Europe
(B) A flow of investment capital from Latin America to Britain
(C) Charitable British development aid with no profit motive
(D) Raw materials out, manufactures in, under foreign financial control
explanation: British capital built the railroads, ports, and mines that carried Argentine wheat and beef, Chilean copper, and Brazilian coffee to world markets — but the profits, the manufactured imports, and the financial control stayed largely in British hands. Latin America exported raw materials and imported finished goods, the classic neocolonial division of labor. (A) is wrong because Latin America industrialized very little in the nineteenth century. (B) is wrong because investment flowed from Britain to Latin America, not the reverse. (C) is wrong because the investments were profit-seeking ventures, not charitable gifts.

stem: Why did the nationalist revolts in the Balkans succeed against the Ottomans in the 1820s when earlier uprisings had failed?
options: (A) The Ottoman army had ceased to exist
(B) The rebels possessed industrially superior weaponry
(C) The Sultan voluntarily granted independence to the Balkan provinces and withdrew his armies
(D) Britain, France, and Russia intervened militarily on the rebels' behalf
explanation: Balkan Christians had risen before and been crushed; what changed in the 1820s was that Britain, France, and Russia sent fleets and armies to aid the Greeks, each hoping to gain from Ottoman dismemberment. Great Power intervention, not rebel strength alone, secured independence. (A) is wrong because the Ottomans still fielded substantial armies. (B) is wrong because the rebels fought mainly with conventional arms of the day, not industrial weaponry. (C) is wrong because the Sultan fought to keep every province; he never endorsed Balkan independence.

stem: Why did British merchants turn to selling opium in China in the early 1800s?
stimulus: A cartoon of the era shows a British officer forcing opium on a Chinese figure, an allusion to the trade imbalance: China bought almost no British manufactured goods, while Britain bought enormous quantities of Chinese tea, silk, and porcelain.
options: (A) The Chinese government requested opium imports
(B) Opium reversed Britain's silver outflow to China
(C) Opium was a legal, taxed import in China
(D) Merchants wanted to spread Christianity in China
explanation: Britain craved Chinese tea, silk, and porcelain, but China wanted almost no British manufactures — so silver flowed steadily east, draining British reserves. Opium, grown in British India, was the one product Chinese consumers would buy in volume, and its sale reversed the silver flow. (A) is wrong because the Chinese government banned opium and fought to suppress it. (C) is wrong because opium was illegal in China; the trade was smuggling, not lawful commerce. (D) is wrong because missionary work was a separate enterprise from the merchants' balance-of-payments motive.

stem: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) created 'treaty ports' in China. What did this system mean in practice?
options: (A) China was partitioned into European colonies governed directly by foreign powers
(B) Foreigners lived under their own laws and treaty-fixed tariffs inside China
(C) The emperor was replaced by a democratic parliament
(D) China withdrew from all foreign trade
explanation: Under the treaty-port system, foreign merchants resided in designated ports under their own consular courts (extraterritoriality) and paid tariffs fixed by treaty rather than by Beijing. China kept its emperor and its territory but lost the sovereign right to govern foreigners and set its own trade taxes within its borders. (A) is wrong because the powers took only Hong Kong outright; they did not partition China into colonies. (C) is wrong because the Qing emperor remained on the throne. (D) is wrong because the treaties forced China open to foreign trade rather than sealing it shut.

stem: In the nineteenth century, non-Western regions typically exported raw materials and imported manufactured goods. Why did this pattern favor the industrialized West?
options: (A) Raw materials exported by non-Western regions were worthless
(B) The West distributed manufactured goods for free as part of a civilizing mission to uplift colonial markets
(C) Non-Western regions refused on principle to build any industry
(D) Manufactured goods commanded higher prices, and the West controlled shipping, finance, and tariffs
explanation: Manufactured goods — textiles, machinery, weapons — sold at far higher prices than the cotton, rubber, and minerals exchanged for them, and Western firms controlled the shipping, insurance, banking, and tariff regimes on top of it. The terms of trade thus transferred wealth steadily toward the industrial core. (A) is wrong because raw materials had real value; the issue was their low price relative to finished goods. (B) is wrong because the West sold manufactures at a profit; nothing was given away. (C) is wrong because many non-Western regions did attempt industry but were blocked by Western tariff and financial power, not by principled refusal.

stem: Beyond doctrine, the Council of Trent ordered bishops to reside in their dioceses and created seminaries to train priests. What problem did these disciplinary reforms address?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Martin Luther's 1520 Address to the Christian Nobility of the German Nation: Luther lays before Germany's princes a program for reforming the Christian estate, driven, he says, not by arrogance but by the distress oppressing all Christendom, especially Germany. Rome, he charges, has built three walls around itself so that no one can reform it, and Christendom has suffered terribly behind them: first, the claim that temporal rulers have no authority over spiritual matters; second, that no one but the pope may interpret the scriptures; third, that no one but the pope may call a council. He then turns to what a true council should address, above all the worldly extravagance of the papacy. It is, he writes, a dreadful thing to see the man who calls himself Christ's vicar living in pomp no king or emperor can match. As for the cardinals, their real function is plain: Italy and Germany hold rich convents, endowments, and benefices, and Rome created cardinals and handed them these prizes as the surest way to drag the wealth into Roman hands, destroying genuine service to God in the process.
options: (A) Overpopulation in the Papal States and the Italian peninsula
(B) A decline in religious art
(C) Absenteeism, corruption, and ignorance among the clergy
(D) Excessive education among priests
explanation: Protestant critics had hammered the Church for absentee bishops who never visited their dioceses, illiterate priests, and the sale of offices. Trent answered by ordering bishops to reside in their sees and creating seminaries to train priests properly.

stem: The map of colonial Africa shows many borders drawn as unnaturally straight lines. What does this reveal about how the borders were created?
stimulus: The map depicts Africa after the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885: the continent partitioned among Britain, France, Germany, Portugal, Belgium, Italy, and Spain. Many interior boundaries run as straight lines across the Sahara and savanna, cutting through regions with no reference to terrain.
options: (A) They were drawn by African rulers themselves
(B) They followed Africa's rivers, lakes, and mountain ranges as natural boundaries
(C) They restored ancient tribal boundaries
(D) Europeans drew them in Berlin without regard to African realities
explanation: Borders drawn by diplomats in Berlin, often with rulers, sliced through kingdoms, language groups, and grazing lands without consultation. Straight lines on the map are the signature of outsiders dividing territory on paper, indifferent to the peoples living there.

stem: After independence, African leaders largely kept the colonial borders rather than redrawing them along ethnic lines. Why?
options: (A) African leaders admired the colonial borders
(B) The United Nations forced Africa to keep them under the decolonization treaties
(C) Leaders did not realize the borders were artificial
(D) Redrawing them would have triggered endless border wars
explanation: Redrawing dozens of borders would have meant war between every new state and its neighbors over every disputed mile. The Organization of African Unity therefore froze the colonial map in 1964, trading the injustice of arbitrary borders for the stability of settled ones.

stem: Colonial powers built African railroads from mines and plantations to ports, but few connecting African cities to each other. What economic pattern did this create?
options: (A) Balanced industrial development across the continent
(B) Dense rail networks linking African cities to each other
(C) African control of international shipping, finance, and commodity marketing
(D) Extractive economies geared to exporting raw materials to Europe
explanation: Colonial railroads ran from the copper mine or the peanut basin straight to the port, built to drain wealth outward, not to connect African producers to African consumers. Independence inherited economies wired to export raw materials and import finished goods.

stem: Dario addresses 'Roosevelt' directly in a 1904 poem denouncing the United States as the 'future invader' of Latin America. Which US policy was he protesting?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Ruben Dario's 1904 poem 'To Roosevelt': You are the United States, the future invader of the native America that has Indian blood, that still prays to Jesus Christ and still speaks Spanish. You think life is fire and progress is eruption, that wherever you aim you strike the future. But our America has had poets since the ancient days of Netzahualcoyotl, has consulted the stars, has lived on light and love since remote times, the America of Montezuma and the Inca, Catholic and Spanish America. It lives, and it dreams, and it loves. Be careful: a thousand cubs of the Spanish lion are loosed. To seize us in your iron claws, Roosevelt, you would need to be God's own hunter. And though you count on everything, you lack one thing: God.
options: (A) The Monroe Doctrine of 1823
(B) American isolationism and principled withdrawal from all foreign entanglements
(C) The Good Neighbor Policy
(D) The Roosevelt Corollary claiming US police power in Latin America
explanation: In 1904 Roosevelt proclaimed the United States an 'international police power' in the Western Hemisphere, entitled to intervene wherever it judged order threatened. Dario, writing as the US detached Panama from Colombia to build the canal, names Roosevelt personally as the embodiment of that doctrine.

stem: Dario contrasts Latin America's spiritual culture with the United States' worship of force and wealth. What literary tradition does this belong to?

explanation: Arielismo, after Shakespeare's airy spirit Ariel, held that Latin America embodied spiritual and cultural values while the Anglo-Saxon north embodied crude materialism, the Caliban of the hemisphere. stem: Parliament's Sadler Committee (1831-32) collected testimony like Joshua Drake's about children working brutal hours for pennies. What was its purpose?
stimulus: Paraphrase of testimony before Parliament's Sadler Committee, 1831-32: Joshua Drake, a working man, is examined. He says he would prefer moderate labor and lower wages, but he has work only two days a week, and jobs pay poorly. A child earning three shillings a week cannot properly subsist on it. Asked why he lets his children work where they are ill-treated and overworked, he answers: necessity compels a man with children to let them work. options: (A) To praise factory conditions
(B) To close Parliament

(D) To recruit young soldiers for the army from among the factory child workers
explanation: The Sadler Committee summoned workers, parents, and overseers to document hours, beatings, and maiming in the mills. Its published testimony shocked the public and gave reformers the evidence they needed to pass the Factory Act of 1833, the first effective child-labor law.

stem: Drake says 'necessity compels' him to send his children to the mills. What economic reality does this describe?

options: (A) Children loved factory work and begged their parents to let them work even longer hours
(B) Parents were simply cruel
(C) Adult wages were too low to support a family, so children's earnings were necessary
(D) Factory wages were generous
explanation: Drake works two days a week at poor wages; his children's mill earnings, miserable as they are, keep the family alive. Child labor was not parental cruelty but household economics: when adult men could not earn a family wage, children had to earn or the family starved.

stem: Britain's Factory Acts (1833, 1844, 1847) limited child labor and the working day. What did they represent?
stimulus: Paraphrase of testimony before Parliament's Sadler Committee, 1831-32: Joshua Drake, a working man, is examined. He says he would prefer moderate labor and lower wages, but he has work only two days a week, and jobs pay poorly. A child earning three shillings a week cannot properly subsist on it. Asked why he lets his children work where they are ill-treated and overworked, he answers: necessity compels a man with children to let them work. He would not send them under the present system if necessity did not force him.
options: (A) State intervention in labor markets, breaking with laissez-faire
(B) They banned all factories
(C) They embodied laissez-faire principles of strict non-interference in labor markets
(D) They applied only to agriculture
explanation: Laissez-faire held that the state should leave labor markets alone; the Factory Acts did the opposite, with inspectors enforcing limits on hours and child labor. Each Act marked Parliament's judgment that unregulated industry produced evils the market would not cure.

stem: Britain's Combination Acts (1799-1800) banned workers' unions, yet by the 1870s unions were legal. Why did Parliament give way?
stimulus: Paraphrase of testimony before Parliament's Sadler Committee, 1831-32: Joshua Drake, a working man, is examined. Asked why he lets his children work where they are ill-treated and overworked, he answers: necessity compels a man with children to let them work. He would not send them under the present system if necessity did not force him.
options: (A) Factory owners demanded unions to improve discipline among workers
(B) Worker pressure and unrest made suppression unenforceable
(C) Unions never actually existed
(D) The king personally ordered it
explanation: The Combination Acts made workers' organizations criminal conspiracies, but strikes, unrest, and the sheer scale of industrial misery kept producing them anyway. Parliament legalized unions in the 1870s because suppression had failed and the organized working class could no longer be ignored.

stem: Kipling wrote 'Gunga Din' while defending the British Empire in India. How does the poem reflect imperial attitudes?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Rudyard Kipling's 'Gunga Din' (1890): The narrator, a British soldier in India, recalls the regiment's bhisti, or water carrier, Gunga Din, a man the soldiers mocked and beat. With only a rag and a goatskin water bag for equipment, Din followed the regiment through every battle, fearless under fire. One night the narrator, wounded and choking with thirst, was found by Din, who gave him foul water, staunched his wound, and carried him to safety, taking a bullet himself. Dying, Din asked only if the narrator liked his drink. The soldier closes: though I beat and cursed you, you are a better man than I am, Gunga Din.
options: (A) It calls for Indian independence and the immediate end of British imperial rule
(B) It ignores India entirely
(C) It portrays Indians as loyal servants valued for their service to the British
(D) It attacks the British army as cruel, incompetent, and unworthy of the Indians' respect
explanation: Gunga Din is praised not as an equal but as the ideal native servant: brave, loyal, self-sacrificing in British service. The poem's affection is real, but it is the affection of a master for a faithful subordinate, the paternalistic core of the imperial imagination.

stem: The narrator closes by admitting he once 'beat and cursed' Gunga Din. What does this admission change about the final tribute?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Rudyard Kipling's 'Gunga Din' (1890): The narrator, a British soldier in India, recalls the regiment's bhisti, or water carrier, Gunga Din, a man the soldiers mocked and beat. With only a rag and a goatskin water bag for equipment, Din followed the regiment through every battle, fearless under fire. One night the narrator, wounded and choking with thirst, was found by Din, who gave him foul water, staunched his wound, and carried him to safety, taking a bullet himself. Dying, Din asked only if the narrator liked his drink. The soldier closes: though I beat and cursed you, you are a better man than I am, Gunga Din.
options: (A) The praise becomes a confession of guilt: the narrator honors a man he himself abused
(B) The narrator reveals he never actually met Gunga Din
(C) The admission proves the narrator promoted Din to officer rank
(D) The poem is really a boast about the narrator's own battlefield heroism
explanation: 'You're a better man than I am' lands differently when the speaker has just confessed to belting and flaying its object. The tribute is not magnanimity from above but guilt from below: the abused native's courage exposes the abuser's moral failure. Kipling turns the imperial hierarchy upside down in the final line, and the confession is what does the turning. (B) is wrong because the narrator describes years of shared service. (C) is wrong because no promotion occurs; Din dies a water carrier. (D) is wrong because the poem's hero is Din, not the narrator.

stem: Kipling also wrote 'The White Man's Burden' urging imperialism. How can 'Gunga Din' seem to criticize imperial arrogance?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Rudyard Kipling's 'Gunga Din' (1890): The narrator, a British soldier in India, recalls the regiment's bhisti, or water carrier, Gunga Din, a man the soldiers mocked and beat. Dying, Din asked only if the narrator liked his drink. The soldier closes: though I beat and cursed you, you are a better man than I am, Gunga Din.
options: (A) Kipling held both beliefs, revealing imperialism's internal tensions
(B) Kipling opposed the British Empire
(C) The two poems were written by different authors holding opposing views on empire
(D) Fiction reveals nothing about real attitudes
explanation: Kipling believed in the empire's civilizing mission and also believed he saw, in men like Din, genuine nobility among the colonized. The two poems together expose imperialism's central tension: a doctrine of racial superiority strained by encounters with individual human worth.

stem: Social Darwinists applied 'survival of the fittest' to nations and races. How did this justify imperialism?
stimulus: Paraphrase of Rudyard Kipling's 'Gunga Din' (1890): The narrator, a British soldier in India, recalls the regiment's bhisti, or water carrier, Gunga Din, a man the soldiers mocked and beat.
